Figure 2:Overview of AnyGoal.Each task preserves the environment dynamics of the corresponding base tasks and keep states and actions individually within training coverage.
Throughout the paper, AnyGoal is used solely as a test set for evaluating generalization.

Figure 4:AnyGoal targets the combinatorial gap.(a) Example factor-wise support check for Avoid-T relative to Push-T using KDE. Darker regions indicate higher density, and gray regions mark areas whose density is below1%1\%of the peak reference density.
(b) Estimated overlap between each target variant and the base-task training distribution via KDE.

Figure 6:Oracle-state predictors reveal dynamics-level failures.Even with task-relevant state factors provided directly, goal shifts still degrade prediction and planning, showing that the AnyGoal gap cannot be reduced to visual representation failure. See AppendixI.1for absolute metrics.

Figure 7:End-to-end degradation reflects representation effects.Compared with oracle-state predictors, end-to-end models degrade more under goal shifts, suggesting additional failures from observation-level shift and learned representation geometry. See AppendixI.1for absolute metrics.

Figure 8:Representation geometry matters under goal shifts.(a) The observations remain visually in support, but end-to-end models degrade while oracle-state predictors remain stable. (b) The 2D t-SNE projections illustrate that learned representations can organize the same underlying agent positions with substantially different geometry, which can affect prediction and planning.

Figure 9:Goal-biased training support is associated with reduced action sensitivity.Each panel plots model action sensitivity against an environment-specific bias coordinate induced by the expert policy. The analysis suggests that the model can partially rely on a goal-directed prior rather than the supplied action.
